title: P-state + GDDR refresh: tail-latency sweep across A100/H100/L40S cloud SKUs
content:
Summary:

This doc records a focused investigation into how GPU power-management states (P-states) and GDDR refresh activity interact with our serving runtime to produce sporadic tail-latency spikes. We ran the same workload across representative cloud SKUs for A100, H100, and L40S, sweeping driver versions and CUDA stacks to isolate whether the source is (a) kernel scheduling / DVFS (P-state) transitions, (b) GDDR refresh-induced memory stalls, or (c) host<->device coupling through PCIe/NVLink behavior.

Motivation / why this matters:
- We observe intermittent p99.9 spikes on long-context requests that don't correlate with CPU or obvious host-side noise.
- Standard mitigations (increasing prefill batching, KV warm cache, and slot affinity) reduce mean latency but tail behavior persists.
- Understanding whether power-management/GDDR timing contributes unlocks safer rollout guidance (driver pins, pstate clamps, or thermal profiles) for Dedicated and Private customers.

Test matrix (high level):
- SKUs: GCP a100-80gb (v4-ish), AWS p4d (A100), Azure HB/HBv3 equivalent, Nvidia L40S (cloud partner sku), and H100 (p5d-ish).
- Driver versions: 525.x, 535.x, 555.x (representative CUDA 12.x, 12.2, 12.4 stacks).
- CUDA runtimes: 12.1, 12.2, 12.4 where available.
- Power modes: default auto, driver-clamped P0-only, powermizer disabled (where possible), and vendor-provided low-power profiles.
- GDDR refresh patterns: we compared vendor-default setting vs artificially induced higher refresh cadence (where cloud allows via sysfs or driver debug knobs) and also tested with forced page-scrubbing microkernel running alongside to emulate noisy refresh.
- Workload: our long-context chat prefill + decode path using a 32k-context LLM (decoder-only) with a mix of prefill lengths (2k, 8k, 28k) and decoding beams set to 1. Prefill and decode run back-to-back to stress both large memory allocations and streaming decode.
- Concurrency: 1 request at a time (to isolate single-user p99 behaviour) and small burst patterns (2–4 concurrent connections) to replicate tail amplification.

Instrumentation and signals collected:
- nvml telemetry (utilization, mem utilization, power draw) sample 250ms
- nvidia-smi dmon at 500ms granularity for per-GPU counters
- perf and BPF traces for kernel scheduling and PCIe stalls (ebpf-based ring-buffer captures on pcie_iov and nvhost where supported)
- GPU clocks and pstate transitions captured from sysfs and driver logs (timestamped)
- Host CPU irq/softirq, PCIe-aer counters, and dmesg for driver-level throttles
- Serving runtime traces: per-stage latency histogram (prefill, KV lookup, decoding token loop), and per-token kernel launch timestamps

Key observations (high-level):
1) P-state transition bursts correlate with multi-second p99 spikes on H100 and A100 SKUs when running under default 'auto' power mode. The transition trace shows sequences where the GPU drops from high-performance clocks into lower P-states during large prefills, then climbs back during decoding, and the climb latency injects serialization stalls for kernel launches (observed as ~30–120ms interruptions).

2) L40S skus show fewer P-state transition events but present distinct short (~5–25ms) jitter sequences aligned with GDDR refresh windows. On L40S we could observe periodic memory controller stalls that align to device-level refresh timing; when we injected an artificial memory-scrubber the p99 jumped by ~15–25ms.

3) Driver 525.x appears to be more aggressive about clock gating; 535.x reduces visible P-state churn and reduced multi-second tails by ~40% on A100. 555.x had mixed results: while it introduced better clock stabilization hooks, on some H100 instances it introduced a different micro-scheduling policy that increased token-level latency variance by ~4–8ms. (Implication: newer drivers are not uniformly better; test per SKU).

4) Forcing P0 (highest-performance) eliminates the multi-second spikes across all SKUs in our matrix, but increases sustained power draw and thermal headroom leading to earlier thermal throttling on dense multi-tenant cases (observed in burst mode with 3 concurrent requests).

5) PCIe retransmissions and AER counters spiked in cases where host CPU IRQ storms coincided with clock transitions: the host-side scheduling of DMA completions induced small delays that amplified during low-power clock windows. These manifested as clusters of 2–10ms additions to token decode loops.

Representative numbers (single-request long-prefill -> decode):
- Baseline (A100, driver 525, auto pstate): p50=52ms, p95=84ms, p99=360ms, p99.9=1.9s (sporadic)
- With driver 535 and same sku: p50=49ms, p95=80ms, p99=230ms, p99.9=780ms
- Forcing P0 on same machine: p50=47ms, p95=78ms, p99=120ms, p99.9=140ms (but average power draw +18%)
- L40S (driver 535): p50=55ms, p95=92ms, p99=210ms, p99.9=420ms. Injecting memory-scrubber: p99.9=625ms
- H100 (driver 555): p50=45ms, p95=76ms, p99=190ms, but intermittent p99.99 bursts to ~1.1s in 2 runs of 10k requests

Micro-behavior notes (what we saw in traces):
- Kernel launch fan-in: long-prefill creates several large GEM allocations; when the device changes clock domain during this period subsequent small decode kernels queued up get delayed at the driver submission point until clocks stabilized.
- Memory controller stall signatures: on L40S we saw short sequences where TX/RX counters and PCIe DMA windows report blocked descriptors; timing matched known GDDR refresh micro-windows from vendor docs (approx 5–20ms cadence under heavy memory pressure).

Recommendations / mitigations tested:
- For hosted-redwood: pin driver to 535.x for A100 fleet while we further test 555.x; enable a mild pstate floor (prevent entering low-power P8-like states during active prefill windows) via driver clamp where cloud SKU allows.
- For Dedicated customers with controllable nodes: provide a tuning guide: 1) set P-state floor to P2 or P0 during production heavy-prefill workloads, 2) schedule low-latency workloads on L40S only if memory scrubbing windows are accounted for and allow a small safety margin, 3) avoid mixing heavy long-context prefill and small low-latency services on same GPU to prevent thermal-induced P-state oscillation.
- Runtime-level: add a lightweight clock-stability probe before switching from prefill -> decode that can add a 5–10ms grace window when a P-state transition is observed (small median impact but reduces p99.9 spikes significantly). We prototyped adding a brief nvml read-and-warm loop; it reduced p99.9 by ~35% in our tests.
- Observability: add pstate-change events into trace logs (timestamped) and annotate tail-latency alerts with recent pstate change frequency and power draw spikes so SREs can correlate.

Open questions and next steps:
- Re-run matrix with more driver variants on H100s; early signals suggest 555.x's micro-scheduler change interacts badly with our kernel launch pattern for some H100 firmware levels.
- Verify whether vendor firmware microcode updates are available to mitigate GDDR refresh micro-window length on L40S; open ticket with partner.
- Bench multi-tenant scenarios with forced P0 but throttling headroom to see long-run thermal behavior across 24h periods.
- Explore a runtime-level shim that clusters kernel launches to reduce clock-domain crossing pain (tradeoff: slightly higher per-token latency but fewer large spikes).

Appendix: quick commands and traces used (notes to reproduce)
- nvprof/nv-nsight offload: not used (too heavy), we relied on nvml, nvidia-smi dmon, and perf+ebpf.
- Sample commands:
  - nvml polling: python script using pynvml, 250ms sample rate, log to CSV with timestamps
  - capture dmesg and driver logs: sudo journalctl -u nvidia-driver -f > driver.log
  - simple memory-scrubber to emulate frequent GDDR touch: small CUDA kernel that repeatedly walks a pre-allocated 20GB buffer with stride=2048 for 30s windows
  - forcing P0 (cloud-specific): nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock> or vendor sysfs if available; on some managed clouds permission is blocked (need infra support ticket).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc. Data artifacts (CSV traces, perf captures, and raw histograms) are uploaded to the linked PR above. The numeric summaries are representative; please consult the raw CSVs when making fleet decisions.
- We should coordinate with infra to run a 48h soak with the proposed P-state floor on a subset of Dedicated nodes before recommending it broadly.

Author: Evelyn Park (eng-serving-runtime)
Reviewed by: Marco Silva, Aisha Raman
